subject: biology
title: Genotype and phenotype
summary: The difference between genotype and phenotype, how dominant and recessive alleles interact in homozygous and heterozygous individuals, and how the environment and epigenetic changes also shape phenotype.
body:
Why do identical twins share all their alleles yet still look and behave a little differently? Why can two brown-eyed parents have a blue-eyed child? The answers come from separating an organism's genotype (its alleles) from its phenotype (what it is actually like), and from seeing how genes and the environment work together.

## Think of it like this

### Phenotype = genotype + environment is like a recipe and the kitchen

Two people follow the exact same banana bread recipe, but one has an oven that runs hot and the other is out of fresh bananas. Their loaves come out a bit different. The recipe is the **genotype**: the alleles that set what is possible. The kitchen (oven, ingredients, time) is the **environment**. The loaf you can see, smell and taste is the **phenotype**. Identical twins are like two cooks with the same recipe in different kitchens, and hydrangea cuttings in acidic and alkaline soil are the same recipe giving blue or pink "loaves".

*Where the analogy breaks down:* a cook can rewrite a recipe, but the environment does not change the genotype; in PKU or hydrangeas, the alleles stay the same and only how they are expressed changes.

### Dominance is like a lamp with two light bulbs

Picture a bedside lamp with two bulbs. If both work, or even if just one works, the room looks lit, so you cannot tell from across the room whether it is TT or **Tt**. Only if both bulbs are dead is the room dark, like the **homozygous recessive** tt phenotype. This matches how a **dominant** allele often works: one working allele makes enough functional protein for a normal phenotype. A **carrier** is the lamp with one dead bulb that still lights the room perfectly.

*Where the analogy breaks down:* not every dominant allele is a "working bulb". Some, like the allele for Huntington's disease, are dominant because they make a harmful protein, and dominant does not mean common or better.

### Epigenetics is like muting an app rather than deleting it

When you mute an app, it is still installed on your phone, exactly as it was, but it stops sending notifications. **Epigenetics** works like that: **DNA methylation** and **histone modification** switch genes off (or on) without changing the DNA base sequence. Tightly wound DNA around histones is like an app buried in a locked folder; loosely wound DNA is like an app on your home screen, easy to use. Just as your habits change which apps you mute, factors like diet, stress and smoking can change epigenetic marks.

*Where the analogy breaks down:* you can unmute an app with one tap, but epigenetic marks are not switched by choice, and some are copied every time a cell divides, so they can last in a tissue for years.

### In real life

Newborn babies in Australia have a heel-prick blood test that checks for PKU, so babies with two faulty alleles can start a low-phenylalanine diet straight away; a change in environment protects their phenotype even though their genotype stays the same. Gardeners also change hydrangea flower colour by adjusting soil pH.

## Key ideas

### Genotype and phenotype

The **genotype** is the combination of alleles an organism has for a particular gene (or, more broadly, all of its genetic information). Because body cells are diploid, an individual has two alleles for each autosomal gene, one on each homologous chromosome.

The **phenotype** is the observable or measurable characteristics of an organism. Phenotype includes obvious features such as flower colour or height, but also things you cannot see directly, such as blood group, enzyme activity or whether a person has a genetic disease.

The relationship can be summed up as:

**phenotype = genotype + environment**

The genotype sets the possibilities; the environment influences which of those possibilities is expressed and to what degree.

### Writing genotypes

Alleles are written as letters. By convention:

- A capital letter stands for the dominant allele (for example **T** for tall).
- The same letter in lower case stands for the recessive allele (**t** for short).
- A genotype has two letters, one for each allele, such as TT, Tt or tt.

Always use the same letter for both alleles of a gene. Writing T for tall and s for short hides the fact that they are versions of one gene.

### Homozygous and heterozygous

- **Homozygous** means the two alleles are the same. TT is **homozygous dominant**; tt is **homozygous recessive**.
- **Heterozygous** means the two alleles are different, as in Tt. A heterozygous individual is sometimes called a hybrid.

### Dominant and recessive alleles

A **dominant** allele is expressed in the phenotype whenever it is present, even if only one copy is there. A **recessive** allele is expressed in the phenotype only when no dominant allele is present, which means the individual must be homozygous recessive.

| Genotype | Description | Phenotype (pea plant height) |
|---|---|---|
| TT | homozygous dominant | tall |
| Tt | heterozygous | tall |
| tt | homozygous recessive | short |

Notice that TT and Tt give the same phenotype. This is why you cannot always tell an organism's genotype from its phenotype. A tall plant could be TT or Tt; a short plant must be tt.

**Why does dominance happen?** It comes down to proteins. Often the dominant allele codes for a working protein, such as an enzyme, and the recessive allele codes for a faulty protein or none at all. In a heterozygote, one working allele usually makes enough of the protein for a normal phenotype. For example, in cystic fibrosis, people with one working copy of the CFTR gene make enough working channel protein to be unaffected; only people with two faulty copies have the condition.

A heterozygous person with a recessive disease allele, but no symptoms, is called a **carrier**.

Dominant does not mean common or better. Some dominant alleles are rare and cause disease, such as the allele that causes Huntington's disease.

### The environment influences phenotype

Many phenotypes depend on the environment as well as the genotype. Some examples:

- **Hydrangea flower colour.** The same plant can produce blue flowers in acidic soil and pink flowers in more alkaline soil, because soil pH affects how much aluminium the plant can take up.
- **Himalayan rabbits and Siamese cats.** These animals have an allele for a temperature-sensitive enzyme involved in making dark pigment. The enzyme works only at cooler temperatures, so dark fur grows on the cooler parts of the body: ears, nose, paws and tail. If a patch of fur is shaved and kept cold, the regrowing fur is dark.
- **Height in humans.** Many genes influence height, but nutrition during childhood also affects how tall a person becomes.
- **Phenylketonuria (PKU).** People with two copies of a faulty allele cannot break down the amino acid phenylalanine. If they follow a low-phenylalanine diet from birth, the harmful effects are largely prevented. The genotype stays the same; the environment (diet) changes the phenotype.

Characteristics controlled by one gene with clear-cut forms (such as pea height or ABO blood group) show **discontinuous variation**: individuals fall into separate categories. Characteristics controlled by many genes plus the environment, such as human height or skin colour, are called **polygenic** and show **continuous variation**: a smooth range of values.

### Epigenetics: an introduction

**Epigenetics** is the study of changes in gene expression that do not involve a change in the DNA base sequence. The genes are still there, but they are switched on or off.

Two main mechanisms:

- **DNA methylation**: methyl groups are attached to DNA, usually near the start of a gene. This generally silences the gene, so it is not transcribed.
- **Histone modification**: chemical groups are added to or removed from histone proteins. This changes how tightly the DNA is wound. Tightly packed DNA is hard to read and genes are switched off; loosely packed DNA is easier to read and genes can be switched on.

These epigenetic marks can be influenced by the environment, including diet, stress, toxins and smoking. Identical twins have the same DNA sequence, but their epigenetic marks become more different as they age and live different lives, which is one reason their phenotypes can differ.

Some epigenetic marks are passed on when cells divide, so they can persist in a tissue. A small number may be passed from parents to offspring, though how often this happens in humans is still being researched.

## Worked examples

### Example 1: Working out genotypes from phenotypes

In guinea pigs, black fur (B) is dominant to white fur (b). A white guinea pig and a black guinea pig have offspring, some of which are white. What is the genotype of each parent?

1. The white parent shows the recessive phenotype, so it must be **bb**.
2. The black parent has at least one B, so it is BB or Bb.
3. Some offspring are white (bb). Each offspring gets one allele from each parent, so a white offspring got a b from the black parent.
4. Therefore the black parent must be **Bb** (heterozygous).

### Example 2: Separating genetic and environmental effects

A student takes cuttings from a single hydrangea plant, so all cuttings have the same genotype. Half are grown in soil at pH 5.5 and half at pH 7.5. Results: the pH 5.5 group produced blue flowers; the pH 7.5 group produced pink flowers.

1. Because cuttings are clones, genotype is controlled (the same in every plant).
2. The only variable changed was soil pH.
3. So the difference in flower colour is caused by the environment, not by different alleles.
4. Conclusion: flower colour phenotype in hydrangeas is influenced by soil pH.

### Example 3: Identical twins with different phenotypes

Identical twins have the same genotype. One twin develops type 2 diabetes in middle age; the other does not.

1. Same DNA sequence, so the difference is not caused by different alleles.
2. Likely causes are environmental factors such as diet and exercise.
3. These factors may also have caused different epigenetic marks, changing the expression of genes involved in blood glucose control.

## Common mistakes

- Assuming a dominant phenotype tells you the genotype. A dominant phenotype could be homozygous or heterozygous; only the recessive phenotype gives a certain genotype.
- Thinking dominant alleles are the most common in a population. Dominance describes how alleles interact in one individual, not how frequent they are.
- Using different letters for alleles of the same gene (such as T and s).
- Saying epigenetic changes alter the DNA sequence. They change gene expression, not the base sequence.
- Saying the environment changes the genotype. In examples like PKU or hydrangeas, the genotype is unchanged; only the phenotype differs.

## Exam tips

- Define genotype and phenotype precisely and give an example of each; vague answers like 'genes' and 'looks' lose marks.
- When explaining dominance, link it to proteins: one working allele can produce enough functional protein.
- For experiment-based questions, explain how genotype was controlled (for example clones or identical twins) so the effect of the environment can be identified.
- For epigenetics, name a mechanism (DNA methylation or histone modification) and state that the DNA sequence is unchanged.

## Tips to remember

- **Genotype = the letters, phenotype = what you see (or measure)**: Tt is a genotype; "tall" is a phenotype.
- **Phenotype = genotype + environment**: genes set the possibilities; the environment influences what actually shows.
- **Homo = same, hetero = different**: TT and tt are homozygous; Tt is heterozygous.
- **Only the recessive tells the truth**: a short plant must be tt, but a tall plant could be TT or Tt. (A made-up memory trick.)
- **Picture a Siamese cat's "cold spots"**: the ears, nose, paws and tail are coolest, so the temperature-sensitive enzyme only makes dark pigment there.
- **Epigenetics = switches, not spelling**: DNA methylation and histone modification switch genes on or off without changing the DNA base sequence. Tightly wound DNA is "locked" and silent.

## Key terms

- **Carrier** — a heterozygous individual who has one copy of a recessive allele but does not show the trait.
- **Continuous variation** — variation with a smooth range of values, usually polygenic and environmentally influenced.
- **Discontinuous variation** — variation that falls into distinct categories.
- **DNA methylation** — adding methyl groups to DNA, usually silencing a gene.
- **Dominant allele** — an allele expressed in the phenotype whenever it is present.
- **Epigenetics** — changes in gene expression that do not involve changes in DNA sequence.
- **Genotype** — the combination of alleles an organism has.
- **Heterozygous** — having two different alleles for a gene.
- **Homozygous** — having two identical alleles for a gene.
- **Phenotype** — the observable or measurable characteristics of an organism.
- **Polygenic** — controlled by many genes.
- **Recessive allele** — an allele expressed only when no dominant allele is present.

## Summary

- Genotype is the alleles an organism has; phenotype is the characteristics it shows.
- Phenotype results from the genotype interacting with the environment.
- A dominant allele shows in the phenotype in both homozygous and heterozygous individuals; a recessive allele shows only when homozygous.
- Dominance often occurs because one working allele makes enough functional protein.
- Environmental factors such as temperature, soil pH and diet can change phenotype without changing genotype.
- Epigenetic changes, such as DNA methylation and histone modification, switch genes on or off without altering the DNA sequence.

questions.prompt: Which term describes an individual with the genotype Rr?
questions.explanation: Rr has two different alleles, so it is heterozygous. Homozygous dominant is tempting because the dominant allele is expressed, but homozygous requires two identical alleles (RR).

questions.prompt: Which of the following is the best definition of phenotype?

options.A: The alleles an organism carries for a gene
options.B: The physical appearance of an organism only
options.C: The observable or measurable characteristics of an organism, including biochemical traits
options.D: The characteristics an organism inherits from its dominant parent

questions.explanation: Phenotype includes anything observable or measurable, including blood group and enzyme activity, not only appearance. Option B is tempting but too narrow, and option A defines genotype.

questions.prompt: Why is a person heterozygous for the cystic fibrosis allele usually unaffected by the disease?

options.A: Their one working allele produces enough functional CFTR protein for normal function
options.B: The recessive allele is destroyed in heterozygous cells
options.C: The recessive allele is only expressed in males
options.D: Heterozygous people produce twice as much CFTR protein as homozygous dominant people

questions.explanation: In a heterozygote, the dominant allele still codes for working protein, and one copy is usually enough for a normal phenotype. Option B is tempting but the recessive allele is still present and passed on; it is simply not shown in the phenotype.

questions.prompt: Siamese cats have dark fur on their ears, paws and tail but pale fur on their body. What is the best explanation?

options.A: Cells in the ears, paws and tail carry different alleles from body cells
options.B: Dark fur alleles are dominant only in the extremities
options.C: Epigenetic changes have altered the DNA sequence in the extremities
options.D: An enzyme needed for dark pigment works only at the cooler temperatures found in the extremities

questions.explanation: The cats carry an allele for a temperature-sensitive enzyme. All body cells have the same genotype, but the enzyme is only active in cooler areas, so the environment (temperature) affects the phenotype. Option A is tempting but all somatic cells have the same alleles.

questions.prompt: Which statement about epigenetic changes is correct?

options.A: They always involve mutations to the base sequence of DNA
options.B: They can switch genes on or off without changing the base sequence of DNA
options.D: They cannot be influenced by the environment

questions.explanation: Epigenetic changes, such as DNA methylation, change whether a gene is expressed, not its sequence. Option A is the most common error; a change in the base sequence is a mutation, not an epigenetic change.

questions.prompt: In pea plants, purple flowers (P) are dominant to white flowers (p). A purple-flowered plant crossed with a white-flowered plant produces some white-flowered offspring. What are the parents' genotypes?
questions.explanation: The white parent must be pp. A white offspring (pp) must have received a p from the purple parent too, so the purple parent is Pp. Option A is tempting, but PP × pp would give only Pp (purple) offspring.

questions.prompt: A person with phenylketonuria (genotype pp) follows a low-phenylalanine diet from birth and develops normally. Which statement is correct?

options.A: The diet has changed the person's genotype to Pp
options.B: The diet has changed the person's phenotype but not their genotype
options.C: The person was never truly homozygous recessive
options.D: The diet has caused the recessive allele to become dominant

questions.explanation: Diet is an environmental factor that changes how the genotype shows itself; the person's alleles remain pp and could be passed on. Option A is tempting but the environment cannot change the alleles a person inherited.

questions.prompt: A researcher wants to show that soil nitrogen affects the height of a plant species, independent of genotype. Which experimental design is best?

options.A: Grow seeds collected from many different wild plants in soils with different nitrogen levels
options.B: Measure the height of wild plants growing in different regions
options.C: Grow one cloned plant in high-nitrogen soil and a different species in low-nitrogen soil
options.D: Grow genetically identical cuttings from one plant in soils with different nitrogen levels, keeping other conditions the same

questions.explanation: Using clones controls genotype, so any difference in height can be linked to nitrogen. Option A is tempting, but seeds from different plants have different genotypes, so genetic differences could explain the results.
